moves.spoken: Back in the ring against a 1580 — and we answer the king-pawn with the Sicilian.
He picks the Alapin, the quiet c3 move. Its whole idea is to build the big center with d4 next. Our job is to preempt that — don't let him roll his pawns to d4 and e4 unchallenged.
The tempting reply is e5, and it's playable — but pushing that pawn leaves the d5-square permanently soft. I'd rather not gift a hole on a central square, so we strike with d5 instead.
teaches: Advancing a pawn concedes the square behind it

moves.spoken: He answers e5 anyway, still angling to follow with d4 and grab space.
So we jam the door shut with d4 of our own, wedging a pawn into his position before he can get there first.
teaches: Contest the center directly with a wedge

moves.spoken: After the trade our pawn sits wedged deep in his half, cramping him and denying the natural central setup he wanted.
The bishop swings out to b5 to pin our knight. We've met this pin a hundred times — the only question is how we choose to break it.
We just quietly unpin with the bishop to d7. Not every piece needs to be doing something heroic — a modest developing move that solves the pin is plenty.
teaches: A quiet unpin is often enough — pieces need not all attack

moves.spoken: d3 here is a very typical mistake, and it's black to play and win. Two alarms should ring: first, loose pieces lie all around, and loose pieces drop off.

Second: the moment a pawn moves near the king, look at the diagonal it just opened. The check on a5 does both jobs at once — it rakes that fresh diagonal and forks the loose bishop, winning a piece outright, because our wedge pawn covers c3 so the knight can't block.
teaches: A pawn move near the king opens diagonals to exploit
Combine a check with an attack on a loose piece

moves.spoken: We scoop up the bishop. A whole piece to the good, and the game is essentially decided.
We grab the central pawn on d3 — though honestly we should have taken on b2, which would have snagged the rook in the corner too. I got greedy for the juicy pawn.
Here's the rule I hammer on: when you win a stack of material, don't forget to develop. Get your pieces out and coordinated instead of gorging on more pawns.
Now a lesson on converting. Trades are good when you're up material — but only take them when they fall in your lap. Never wreck your position just to force one.
teaches: Trade when ahead, but only when it comes for free

moves.spoken: His queen lands on d6 and it's actually trappable — Qc5 would hunt it — but there's something even cleaner.
The knight jumps to f5, hitting the queen and forcing the trade back on our terms. The extra material carries the game.
Into the endgame, and the same rules hold: consolidate first. We recapture and keep everything tidy.
teaches: Consolidate before converting in the endgame

moves.spoken: The bishop redeploys to c6, its most active diagonal, doing real work rather than sitting home.
teaches: Put pieces on their most active squares

moves.spoken: King to e7 — in the endgame the king is a fighter. No need to castle; walking it toward the center improves the coordination between our pieces.
teaches: Centralize the king in the endgame

moves.spoken: Careful: dropping the bishop to b7 would run into a nasty rook check on c7. We sidestep to d7 instead, which also forces the rook trade.
teaches: Check for tactical replies before developing

moves.spoken: Now the textbook conversion: pick a wing, make a passed pawn, and use the extra bishop to keep dislodging his blockading rook until it has to give way — then push the pawn home. And with a winning position, watch for stalemate before you finish.
plans: Create a passed pawn and escort it
Use the extra piece to evict the blockader

moves.spoken: On the recap: after exd5 and the queen recapture, this looks like a Scandinavian — but it's better for us. The difference is the extra c3-pawn: it blocks White's own knight from c3, so he can't develop with tempo by hitting the queen.
teaches: The c3-pawn denies White the Nc3 tempo on the queen

moves.spoken: There's a real theoretical line with d4 and Nf6 where it's genuinely unclear who stands better — a rich, double-edged position on both sides.

The through-line of the game: we wedged the pawn to d4 to stop his French-style plans, and his key slip d3 walked into the fork. And note the counter-idea — a pin cuts both ways; the bishop's own pin can be turned against it with the knight grabbing on e5.
teaches: A pin works both ways — the pinner can be exploited too
